# Learning the Platform, Not the Learner: Sequencing Shortcuts in the Offline Evaluation of Educational Recommender Systems and LLM Rankers
## 1 Introduction
This paper asks a simple question: when a recommender or an LLM scores well on such logs, has it learned the learner or the platform? Put differently, *can recommenders and LLMs beat the syllabus?*, where by the syllabus we mean, broadly, the sequencing that the course and the platform impose: the course order, the grouping of activities into problem sets, parts or topics, and the typical paths that assignments produce.

context.title: Endless video feeds leave users with ADHD struggling to stop, survey finds
context.snippet:
Short-form video platforms such as TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts use an effective tactic to maximize the time their users spend on the platforms: They feed one video after another into an algorithmically generated feed. As you scroll, new content loads automatically. This creates an endless loop of ever-changing content with no discernible end.
Such inclusive features could help to mitigate the negative effects of the engagement trap in the long term and strengthen digital self-determination. Platform operators under pressure These scientific findings from TU Graz come against the backdrop of an increasingly public, political and legal debate over whether platform operators such as Meta encourage compulsive or potentially addictive use through certain design elements and recommendation systems, thereby breaching their duty of care. In the U.S., Meta and Google were found negligent by a jury in a landmark case in March 2026 and ordered to pay a total of $6 million in damages; TikTok and Snapchat had previously reached out-of-court settlements with the plaintiff. Developments have also taken concrete shape at the EU level: The European Commission identified preliminary breaches of the Digital Services Act by TikTok in February 2026 and by Instagram and Facebook in July 2026 due to "addictive" designs. The focus is, among other things, on infinite scrolling, autoplay, push notifications and personalized recommendation systems, as well as their potential impact on physical and mental health, particularly that of minors and vulnerable adults. # beat-the-syllabus

Structural baselines and lift-over-structure reports for the offline evaluation of educational recommender systems. Companion code of Learning the Platform, Not the Learner: Sequencing Shortcuts in the Offline Evaluation of Educational Recommender Systems and LLM Rankers (Youssef Jdidou, arXiv:2611.33240).

In logs of tutoring systems, learning applications and MOOCs, the next activity is largely decided by the platform. A recommender can therefore score well offline by reproducing the platform's sequencing. This package measures how much of a recommender's accuracy the sequencing alone already gives, with four predictors that know nothing about the learner beyond the last activity:

Predictor | What it recommends 
---|---
POP | the activities most training learners did 
ORDER | the activities that come next in the course order estimated from the training learners 
CONT | the unseen activities of the last activity's container (problem set, unit, chapter), in course order 
MC | the activities that most often followed the last activity (first-order transitions)

# Does It Look Sequential? An Analysis of Datasets for Evaluation of Sequential Recommendations

###### Abstract.

Sequential recommender systems are an important and demanded area of research. Such systems aim to use the order of interactions as time \(r\) allows by a predict future interactions. The premise is that the order of interactions and sequential patterns play an essential role. Therefore, it is crucial to use datasets that exhibit a sequential structure to evaluate sequential recommenders properly.

Our findings show that several popular datasets have a rather weak sequential structure.

# Towards Realistic Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification for LLM-Based Recommender Systems

Not on the map. Why?

## Abstract (arXiv)

Large language models (LLMs) provide a flexible interface for recommendation systems. However, their issued rankings require reliable instance-level uncertainty monitoring. In this scenario, comparing uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods becomes challenging because LLM rankers lack a standard item-classification head. Their scores may depend on option labels, prompts, generation procedures, and the available user and item evidence. Existing methods derive uncertainty from different sources and apply it at different stages of the recommendation process. Some methods evaluate an issued ranking, whereas others use uncertainty to change the ranking itself, making direct comparison difficult. Here we introduce a fixed-ranking benchmark which evaluates eight heterogeneous UQ signals as record-level monitors under a shared output contract. We evaluate these signals across four recommendation datasets and two LLM backbones under a shared fixed-ranking protocol. From the results, we draw three main observations. First, UQ method ordering changes across backbones even on the same reference instances. Second, ranking-aligned Top10Mass provides the strongest scalar Error@10 detection in several evaluation conditions, reflecting effective cutoff-aligned monitoring, while its advantage narrows for popularity-tail targets. Third, scalar UQ signals are weak at identifying which control has the larger clipped NDCG@10 difference, whereas source-specific signals, including Perturbation Rank Instability and simple listwise distances, provide stronger paired-control agreement, reflecting their sensitivity to the two controlled evidence sources. These findings motivate us to evaluate ranking-failure detection, robustness across recommendation conditions, and responses to controlled evidence changes as distinct properties of UQ.

> Abstract:The technical foundations of recommender systems have progressed from collaborative filtering to complex neural models and, more recently, large language models. Despite these technological advances, deployed systems often underserve their users by simply presenting a list of items, leaving the burden of exploration, comparison, and synthesis entirely on the user. This paper argues that this traditional "tool-based" paradigm fundamentally limits user experience, as the system acts as a passive filter rather than an active assistant. To address this limitation, we propose a novel deep research paradigm for recommendation, which replaces conventional item lists with comprehensive, user-centric reports. We instantiate this paradigm through RecPilot, a multi-agent framework comprising two core components: a user trajectory simulation agent that autonomously explores the item space, and a self-evolving report generation agent that synthesizes the findings into a coherent, interpretable report tailored to support user decisions. This approach reframes recommendation as a proactive, agent-driven service. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that RecPilot not only achieves strong performance in modeling user behaviors but also generates highly persuasive reports that substantially reduce user effort in item evaluation, validating the potential of this new interaction paradigm.

ABSTRACT
Latent reasoning in generative recommendation faces two practical barriers: con-
structing teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision is costly, and re-
current hidden-state feedback requires a specialized execution loop. We revisit
both the supervision source and the computation interface. A step-level diagno-
sis measures how recommendation CoT supports next-item prediction and trace
coherence. In the analyzed traces, history analysis is the only step with positive
mean contributions on both dimensions, while later preference and intent steps
have negative mean answer contributions. Guided by this finding, we propose
PHiT (Prefilled, History-Informed Thought Tokens), which learns intermediate
states from semantic targets extracted directly from observed item histories. PHiT
aggregates cached sparse item encodings to construct these targets and supervises
the contextual states of distinct vocabulary thought tokens. All thought tokens are
supplied together as ordinary input IDs during a single causal prefill, removing the
need for recurrent final-state feedback. With supervised fine-tuning alone, PHiT
outperforms the compared baselines across four recommendation benchmarks. Con-
trolled ablations support the value of input-matched semantic supervision, while
cost measurements show fast target construction with training time comparable to
the recommendation-only thought-token baseline.

Platform Competition Benefit Users?

Abstract
Conventional recommender systems operate within platform-specific catalogs, limiting
access to potentially valuable resources across platforms. We propose user-centered agentic
recommendation, a paradigm in which user agents compare recommendations from competing
platform agents, and formalize their interaction as a repeated game. Platforms strategically
modify descriptions without changing intrinsic item value, while each user agent assesses
platform credibility using feedback from consumed items only. Our analysis shows that
expanded resource access need not improve user welfare: strategic misrepresentation and
limited verification can offset the benefits of platform competition. We quantify when
platform credibility assessment allows users to benefit from broader access despite strategic
exaggeration. Our analysis identifies resource and reporting conditions that guarantee higher
average welfare than the original platform with an interaction budget linear in platform
count. Experiments on synthetic and Amazon-grounded markets show that credibility
assessment can improve finite-horizon utility, while its benefits depend on market size and
mechanism parameters.

In this work, we propose user-centered agentic recommendation: a personal user agent
solicits recommendations from multiple platform agents to find the most relevant resource
on the user’s behalf. Each platform retains its private catalog and responds independently.
The user agent brings these responses together at the point of choice, without requiring
competitors to share catalogs or a central service to control their resources.

Platform Competition Benefit Users?

Abstract
Conventional recommender systems operate within platform-specific catalogs, limiting
access to potentially valuable resources across platforms. We propose user-centered agentic
recommendation, a paradigm in which user agents compare recommendations from competing
platform agents, and formalize their interaction as a repeated game. Platforms strategically
modify descriptions without changing intrinsic item value, while each user agent assesses
platform credibility using feedback from consumed items only. Our analysis shows that
expanded resource access need not improve user welfare: strategic misrepresentation and
limited verification can offset the benefits of platform competition. We quantify when
platform credibility assessment allows users to benefit from broader access despite strategic
exaggeration. Our analysis identifies resource and reporting conditions that guarantee higher
average welfare than the original platform with an interaction budget linear in platform
count. Experiments on synthetic and Amazon-grounded markets show that credibility
assessment can improve finite-horizon utility, while its benefits depend on market size and
mechanism parameters.

In this work, we propose user-centered agentic recommendation: a personal user agent
solicits recommendations from multiple platform agents to find the most relevant resource
on the user’s behalf. Each platform retains its private catalog and responds independently.
The user agent brings these responses together at the point of choice, without requiring
competitors to share catalogs or a central service to control their resources.

octen.title: Hard Negative Sampling via Large Language Models for Recommendation
octen.snippet: Hard negative sampling improves recommendation performance by accelerating convergence and sharpening the decision boundary. However, most existing methods rely on heuristic strategies, selecting negatives from a fixed candidate pool. Lacking semantic awareness, these methods often misclassify items that align with users' semantic interests as negatives, resulting in False Hard Negative Samples (FHNS). Such FHNS inject noisy supervision and hinder the model's optimal performance. To address this challenge, we propose HNLMRec, a generative semantic negative sampling framework. Leveraging the semantic reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), HNLMRec directly generates negative samples that are behaviorally distinct yet semantically relevant with respect to user preferences. Furthermore, we integrate collaborative filtering signals into the LLM via supervised fine-tuning, guiding the model to synthesize more reliable and informative hard negatives. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that HNLMRec significantly outperforms traditional methods and LLM-enhanced baselines, while effectively mitigating popularity bias and data sparsity, thereby improving generalization. cs.IR Chu Zhao, En-Neng Yang, Yuting Liu, Jian-Zhe Zhao, Gui-Bing Guo

octen.title: Cross-attention Secretly Performs Orthogonal Alignment in Recommendation Models
octen.snippet: Cross-domain sequential recommendation (CDSR) aims to align heterogeneous user behavior sequences collected from different domains. While cross-attention is widely used to enhance alignment and improve recommendation performance, its underlying mechanism is not fully understood. Most researchers interpret cross-attention as residual alignment, where the output is generated by removing redundant and preserving non-redundant information from the query input by referencing another domain data which is input key and value. Beyond the prevailing view, we introduce Orthogonal Alignment, a phenomenon in which cross-attention discovers novel information that is not present in the query input, and further argue that those two contrasting alignment mechanisms can co-exist in recommendation models We find that when the query input and output of cross-attention are orthogonal, model performance improves over 300 experiments. Notably, Orthogonal Alignment emerges naturally, without any explicit orthogonality constraints. Our key insight is that Orthogonal Alignment emerges naturally because it improves scaling law. We show that baselines additionally incorporating cross-attention module outperform parameter-matched baselines, achieving a superior accuracy-per-model parameter. We hope these findings offer new directions for parameter-efficient scaling in multi-modal research. cs.LG, cs.IR Hyunin Lee, Yong Zhang, H. ## Introduction

Understanding the role that social media has in the radicalization of extremists has gained an increasing amount of attention from the research community. A new paper on this, titled Algorithmic Extremism: Examining YouTube’s Rabbit Hole of Radicalization, hit arXiv this week, and has caused a bit of a stir on social media.

Abstract

In traditional recommender systems (RSs), textual information typically serves as auxiliary signals for representation learning. In contrast, in LLM-based RSs, textual information becomes the primary medium for recommendation generation through semantic understanding and reasoning. This shift fundamentally changes the attack surface, making promotion-driven manipulations more feasible, effective, and harder to detect. However, effectively detecting such attacks remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we present the first systematic study on detecting promotion-driven attacks against LLM-based RSs, aiming to safeguard next-generation recommendation platforms. Specifically, we propose GuardAgent, a novel LLM-powered agentic detection framework that operates through a loop of Perception, Action, Reflection and Memory. In contrast to conventional LLM-based detectors that function in a static, one-off, and opaque fashion, GuardAgent continually learns and self-evolves to adapt to unseen threat patterns while generating explainable reasoning traces and outcomes. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that GuardAgent achieves state-of-the-art generalization performance, laying the foundation for robust and trustworthy recommendation in practical settings.

corpus.title: Learning the Platform, Not the Learner: Sequencing Shortcuts in the Offline Evaluation of Educational Recommender Systems and LLM Rankers
corpus.snippet: Educational recommenders are usually compared offline, by how well they predict the next activity in logs of tutoring systems, learning applications and MOOCs, where the next activity is largely decided by the platform: teachers assign problem sets, tutors draw problems until mastery, engines select questions. On eight public datasets from five platforms, we compare four structural predictors, which use nothing about the learner beyond the last activity, with ten personalised recommenders and with open-weight LLM rankers from 0.5 to 7 billion parameters, under two protocols. The structural predictors reach between 0.81 and 1.00 of the best accuracy of any method (median 0.95), mostly through population transitions rather than the course order; the best personalised recommender is significantly better on five datasets, by 0.007 to 0.102 NDCG@10, and on Eedi in three of four training runs. Every method is far less accurate on steps along transitions never seen in training and on steps chosen by learners. LLM rankers look competent with random negatives but are never much better than a word-matching baseline, and with negatives that are plausible under the course structure they stay close to random or well behind the transition heuristic, whatever their size. In a simulation with known learner needs, the structural share tracks the share of steps decided by the platform, and offline accuracy ranks an oracle of the learners' needs below imitators of the platform. Weighting test steps by how unlikely the structure makes them restores much of the link with usefulness and, on the real data, reveals a significant personalisation signal on seven of the eight datasets. We propose a syllabus-aware evaluation checklist and release a Python package that reports the lift of any recommender over the structure.

corpus.title: VirusCascade: Hijacking Collaborative Reflection in LLM-Powered Recommender Agents
corpus.snippet: Advancing beyond traditional static scoring models, LLM-powered agentic recommender systems (LLM-ARS) instantiate users and items as autonomous agents, whose semantic states are dynamically refined through a recurrent process known as collaborative reflection. While this mechanism improves recommendation quality, it simultaneously introduces a systemic vulnerability: adversarial evidence injected into a single agent can be rationalised into a legitimate preference narrative, written back into memory, and propagated to other agents through interaction contexts. We term the local rationalisation process reflection laundering, and its system-wide escalation through collaborative reflection collaborative-reflection hijacking. Existing attacks on recommender systems, whether based on interaction-level data poisoning or text-level adversarial perturbations, assume static pipelines and thus cannot exploit this recurrent, multi-agent amplification pathway. To bridge this gap, we first conduct a controlled vulnerability analysis that establishes two exploitable properties underlying collaborative-reflection hijacking: reflective persistence and cross-agent propagation. Then building on these findings, we propose VirusCascade, the first black-box targeted promotion attack that jointly shapes semantic and structural attack surfaces: the former ensures the target item is naturally rationalised as satisfying broad user preferences, the latter positions it for system-wide propagation. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets across diverse LLM-ARS architectures demonstrate that VirusCascade consistently achieves state-of-the-art targeted exposure under evaluated stealth constraints, reaching a mean E@20 of 0.384 and surpassing the strongest baseline by an absolute margin of +0.185.

corpus.title: ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$: Temporal Distribution Shift Generalization for Industry-Scale Recommender Systems
corpus.snippet: Temporal distribution shift (TDS) degrades the generalization of recommender systems: models trained on past interactions face systematically different user behavior in future time windows. While incremental training on recent data is widely used in industrial production, it can over-adapt to transient patterns and exacerbate instability. Existing approaches such as invariant learning and self-supervised learning offer partial solutions but often suffer from unstable temporal generalization, representation collapse, or inefficient data utilization. To address these limitations, we propose ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$, a probabilistic framework for temporally robust recommendation. First, we identify key shifting factors in real-world production data and design a simple yet effective data augmentation strategy that simulates realistic time-varying factors and expands the training support. Second, we derive a self-supervised variational objective, ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$, to harness the benefits of this extended distribution while preventing representation collapse. Extensive experiments on both a public benchmark and a large-scale industrial dataset demonstrate that ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$ consistently improves next-period ranking performance over strong baselines. It achieves a 2.33\% uplift in GMV per user in online experiments and has been successfully deployed in production. Code is available at this https URL
